title: An Ant's Random Walk on a Cube | AMC 8-Style Level 4

lines: An ant takes three random steps along the edges of a cube.
How likely is it to end up at the far corner? <short pause> Let's find out!
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's crack it together.
Here's the question.
An ant stands on a corner of a cube.
Each minute, it walks along an edge to one of the three nearest corners.
Each of those three corners has the same chance.
What is the probability that after three minutes, it's at the corner farthest from its start?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.
Let's name the corners. The ant starts at corner A.
The corner farthest from A is G, at the opposite end of the cube.
The ant takes exactly three steps. We want the chance that it ends at G.
Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
Welcome back! Let's sort the corners by how many edges they are from A.
B, D and E are next to A. They're one edge away.
C, F and H are two edges away. And G is three edges away.
Here's the key. The ant has only three steps, and G is three edges away.
So every step must take it farther from A. If it ever steps back, it runs out of steps.
Step one: from A, all three edges lead away. The chance is three over three, which is one.
Step two: say the ant went to B. From D or E, the picture is just the same.
From B, one edge goes back to A, and two go farther away. That's two over three.
Step three: say it's at C now. Two edges go back, and only one goes to G. That's one over three.
All three steps must go right, one after another. So we multiply the chances.
One, times two over three, times one over three,
is two over nine. That's choice C!
Here's another way. Let's count every possible walk.
Each minute, the ant has three choices. Three times three times three is twenty-seven walks.
All twenty-seven walks are equally likely. So how many of them end at G?
Think of the edges as three directions: across, up, and in.
To get from A to G, the ant must go across once, up once, and in once.
Going the same direction twice cancels out. Then three steps can't cover all three directions.
So every good walk is one order of those three moves.
Three choices for the first move, two for the second, one for the last. That's six walks.
Here are all six routes, drawn on the cube.
Six out of twenty-seven is six over twenty-seven. That's two over nine. It matches!
Look! Three, two, one on top, and three, three, three below. The same numbers as before.
When would you pick this way? When the walks are easy to list, it's a great double-check.
Now, let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
One over twenty-seven is one over three, three times. It treats every step like step three.
But step one is always safe, and step two has two good edges. There are six routes, not one.
One over nine is what you'd get if step two had only one good edge. But it has two.
One over three is what you'd get if you only looked at the last step.
Four over nine is what you'd get if the last step had two good edges. Only one reaches G.
So here's a great habit. At each step, count only the edges that keep you on track.
Ready for a challenge? Here's a sleepy ant on the same cube.
Each minute, it walks along one of the three edges, or it naps and stays put.
All four choices are equally likely. What's the chance it's at G after three minutes?
Pause the video, and go for it!
Let's check. G is still three edges away, and there are still three minutes.
So the ant can't nap at all! Every step must move away from A.
Now each minute has four choices, not three.
The chances are three over four, then two over four, then one over four.
Multiply them: six over sixty-four,
which is three over thirty-two.
Count check: four times four times four is sixty-four walks, and the same six routes work.
If you found three over thirty-two, amazing work!
Here's the big idea to remember.
At each step, ask which moves keep you on the path, and find that chance.
Then multiply the chances along the path.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
